Museums Victoria biography reports a sale to a London brewery in 1857; its reproduced Smithsonian label identifies the ether-compression machine family. This is a sale, not inferred machine operation or worldwide first.

IOR p. 6 says the ammonia machine ran reliably at Marshall in April 1874; Texas State Historical Association gives Jefferson and winter 1873–74. Ice sales rose later in summer. Exact geography and chronology remain qualified.

Fischer 1877 pp. 172–173 describes a Linde machine allowing ammonia or methyl ether and a working Sedlmayer plant. The 1886 report associates an ammonia unit with this brewery, while the individual charge and start are not independently identified.
The 1886 account reports 340 Linde-system installations across named industries; this is its own unaudited count, not a measure of global share or proof of the refrigerant of every installation.

The issue dated 18 December 1868 prints Shand’s discussion of Tellier’s cooled chamber and ammonia and Paul’s belief that ammonia was mechanically recompressed. The issue date is not asserted to be the meeting or machine-use date.

Fischer p. 173 says Augsburg supplied the described Linde line in seven sizes at prices; the XML represents numerical cells as a figure, and the general description permits ammonia or methyl ether. No sale or specific unit charge is inferred.
Schmidt 1882 p. 89 explicitly describes Linde developing the compression system previously commonly used with ether; it is not a claim that a particular 1857 machine caused Boyle or Linde designs.

structural_composition_rule: Owned event IDs and provenance.source_ids are deterministic unions of already accepted event/anchor/lifecycle/patch evidence. They make no new historical claim.

baseline.research_scope: Continuing C wave: closed vapor-compression refrigeration and the ammonia working-fluid branch.

cases.comparison_subject: A closed fluid circuit mechanically recompresses a phase-changing refrigerant, condenses it and returns liquid to the evaporator.

comparators.configuration: Cullen/Leslie vacuum evaporation and chemical freezing mixtures
comparators.contrast: Earlier refrigeration and ice-making methods already existed; the candidate specifically combines mechanical vapor compression, condensation and repeated circulation.

comparators.configuration: Ammonia–water absorption and permanent-gas cold-air machines
comparators.contrast: Absorption uses a solvent/heat-based cycle and gas expansion machines use permanent gas; the candidate is a mechanical compressor applied to a condensing volatile refrigerant. Historical comparative performance depends on assumptions.

cases.limits: A 2011 article reports an 1851 ether prototype installation at a Bendigo brewery, but cites a 2004 retrospective; another institutional history dates a Bendigo installation to 1860. It is not established whether these refer to the same machine or whether the 1851 prototype was in brewery use. Twining’s own machine operated intermittently in Cleveland from 1855 according to a 1902 retrospective; its status as experimental versus a broader customer use is unresolved. The 1857 sale is a local transaction, not a claim of worldwide first sale or invention. Perkins’s 1834 patent and 1835 demonstration precede it.
cases.identity_check: Current canonical labels and configurations do not contain this broad closed vapor-compression architecture; the separately accepted Bell–Coleman air cycle uses a different working cycle.

cases.comparison_subject: Mechanical vapor compression with ammonia as a refrigerant, with pressure and equipment implications compared with ether.

comparators.contrast: The broad mechanical cycle already existed; ammonia is a distinct working-fluid configuration. Schmidt attributes smaller cylinder volume and avoidance of inward air leakage to its higher vapor pressure under his considered conditions.

comparators.configuration: Earlier ammonia/water absorption and hybrid machines
comparators.contrast: Ammonia was used earlier in absorption-based refrigeration; this branch uses a mechanical compressor to circulate ammonia vapor and is not the invention of ammonia cooling in general.

comparators.configuration: Earlier Beath, Tellier and De Coppet ammonia work
comparators.contrast: The 1868 Beath construction claim and earlier Tellier or Merz work may predate the selected Texas operation. Their exact working and community-use chronology is not settled by the inspected sources.

cases.limits: A 2022 engineering history locates reliable operation in Marshall in April 1874 after serious leaks at Jefferson, with ice sales increasing over the summer, while the Texas historical account describes a Jefferson plant and 1873–74 improvements. The exact chronology and operating site therefore remain qualified. An ASHRAE chronology reports a Beath ammonia-compression plant in 1868 but the detailed 2022 study associates Beath’s documented successful systems with absorption. Tellier’s ammonia operation was discussed in 1868, and De Coppet was engaged at Merz brewery in 1869; the date of the subsequent successful compressor’s use is not securely fixed by the inspected source. The 1872 Boyle patent does not identify ammonia. No claim of global invention or first machine sale is made.
cases.identity_check: No existing node describes ammonia as the working fluid in a mechanical compression cycle. The broader compression-cycle node is included separately as an enabling architecture; regional installations are events rather than extra nodes.

frontier_scope: Exact independently reviewed configuration comparisons. Only accepted proposed records enter the canonical graph; held leads and excluded candidates in supporting context are unresolved research, not additional accepted facts. No exhaustive worldwide priority survey is claimed.
